Chapter Two: The Power of Curiosity When the Old Answers Fail
You know, when life’s old routines suddenly stop working, it’s so tempting to chase after quick fixes. That feeling of not knowing—of being caught off guard or out of place—it can be really uncomfortable.
But what if, instead of rushing to patch things up, you leaned into curiosity? Imagine shifting from a desperate need to be sure, to simply asking questions. That small change can turn even the most unsettling moments into something new—even exciting.
Let me share a story. Picture a parent, fresh in a noisy new city, watching their once-bold child suddenly pull back—too shy to join the playground, quiet in class. The parent wants nothing more than to make it better: to offer advice, to reassure. But, no matter what they say, it just doesn’t help.
One afternoon, after another tough day, they sit together on a park bench. This time, instead of trying to fix things, the parent asks, “What’s something you’re curious about here?”
At first, there’s silence. Then, the child looks up and wonders—out loud—about the pigeons in the park. Where do they sleep? What do they eat? How do they find their way home?
Suddenly, the whole mood shifts—from anxiety to wonder. For a moment, neither of them feels weighed down by not having answers.
Curiosity, as it turns out, is a powerful antidote to fear. Most of us, when we’re unsure, slip into self-criticism or just avoid the situation altogether. We beat ourselves up for not knowing, or we fall back on old habits.
But curiosity? It lets you make mistakes. It makes room for awkwardness, for learning at your own pace. Suddenly, the unknown isn’t some looming threat—it’s an adventure waiting to unfold.
Here’s another example. Think of someone who’s always felt competent, suddenly thrown into a brand new job where nothing makes sense. The systems, the culture—everything feels like a pop quiz they’re failing.
At first, they’re frustrated. But slowly, they start treating each confusion like a puzzle instead of a problem. They ask questions—even when they’re basic, or a little embarrassing. And you know what? People respond with kindness. The job goes from intimidating to inviting. Just by saying, “I don’t know, but I’d like to learn,” the whole experience changes.
Most of us underestimate what happens when we ask new questions. There’s all this pressure to look like we’ve got it together. But real growth? That starts with having the courage to admit, “I haven’t learned that yet.”
And this isn’t just for the big moments. It shows up in everyday life—trying a new recipe, having a tough conversation, or making friends in a new place. Curiosity opens doors that certainty keeps shut.
Over time, making curiosity a habit changes everything. It softens fear, and lets in little sparks of joy—even when things feel uncertain.
It’s not about having all the answers, but about being open to the next question.
So, let curiosity walk with you through change. It’s a gentle reminder—it’s okay not to know, as long as you’re willing to learn.
